narrative:
The model determined that you have an 81.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest factors pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of roughly the sixth and fifth deciles among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model that you would likely struggle with the bar exam.

Your family income level was the third most important factor, but it worked mildly in the opposite direction. Being from an upper-middle-income background slightly nudged the prediction toward success, consistent with patterns seen in many accepted applicants.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic standing in law school outweighed the positive signal from your background, producing a high probability of bar failure.

You should focus on strengthening the academic skills measured by the bar exam. Consider enrolling in a structured bar-preparation course, working with a tutor on your weakest subjects, and taking several full practice exams to identify and close knowledge gaps before retaking the exam or reapplying.
